newsitem.title: USA: U.S. bank reform alters broker exams for banks.
newsitem.headline: U.S. bank reform alters broker exams for banks.

text.p: The House Banking Committee on Friday backed off a previously approved amendment to financial sector reform legislation that would have required banks selling securities to join the National Association of Securities Dealers.

By voice vote, the panel approved an amendment to require bank employees to take NASD exams and continuing education programs, but under the auspices of federal bank regulators. The employees would not be subject to NASD disciplinary proceedings and banks would not be monitored by NASD auditors.

On Thursday, the panel approved an amendment by Texas Democrat Ken Bentsen requiring banks that sell securities to join the NASD, a private organization that enforces some securities regulations under authority from the Securities and Exchange Commission.

Under current law, the conduct of employees of brokerage firms who sell securities is overseen by the NASD. Bank employees who sell securities are not overseen by the NASD, although federal bank regulators have proposed requiring such workers to pass the brokerage exams. The employees would still not be subject to NASD disciplinary proceedings.
Banking groups had strongly opposed Bentsen's amendment, which they said would subject banks to broad NASD regulation, requiring record keeping and auditing, even for ordinary banking activities.

The banking committee is in its fourth and final day of debate on legislation to overhaul antiquated U.S. banking laws and allow banks to combine with insurance companies and securities firms. The panel is expected to vote on the entire bill later in the day, but even if the bill is approved, substantial hurdles remain before it could become law.
